s: Concave pole pieces with a soft-iron cylinder inside the coil make the field radial.
In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so the torque NIAB is the same at every position and the deflection is proportional to the current.
mcqs.n: The soft-iron core also concentrates (strengthens) the field, so some keys give D; the purpose of making the pole pieces concave is to make the field radial.

shortQuestions: The charged plastic rod is at rest, so it produces only an electric field, not a magnetic field.
The deflection is electrostatic: the rod's field polarises (induces charges on) the needle and attracts it. It is not a magnetic effect.
Permeability μ measures how easily a medium supports magnetic field lines (B = μH); unit H m⁻¹. For free space μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹.
Permittivity ε measures how a medium affects (reduces) the electric field and electric force between charges, F = q₁q₂/(4πεr²); unit F m⁻¹ (C² N⁻¹ m⁻²). For free space ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.
Permeability belongs to magnetism; permittivity belongs to electrostatics.
Yes — a rotating object produces a magnetic field if it carries charge, because moving charges form a current.
Examples: a charged disc or sphere spinning about its axis; the rotation of the Earth's molten iron core produces the Earth's magnetic field; spinning and orbiting electrons make atoms magnetic.
Both have the same charge magnitude e and speed v, so the force F = evB is the same.
Radius r = mv/(eB): the electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, so its path has a much smaller radius.
Hence the electron suffers the greater deflection (it also curves the opposite way).
Yes. If the particle moves parallel or anti-parallel to B, F = qvB sin θ = 0 and it continues in a straight line.
It can also go straight in a non-zero B if an electric force qE exactly balances qvB (crossed fields, velocity selector).

Parallel currents in the same direction attract, so the turns pull together and the spring contracts.

A cyclotron accelerates only charged particles (protons, deuterons, α-particles); fast neutrons are produced indirectly, e.g. by striking a target with accelerated deuterons.
The loop turns until its plane is perpendicular to B, i.e. its magnetic moment m = NIA is parallel to B.
In this position the torque τ = m × B is zero and the equilibrium is stable (potential energy −mB is minimum).
A current-carrying coil produces a magnetic field like that of a bar magnet: lines emerge from one face and enter the other.
The face where the current appears anticlockwise acts as a north pole and the clockwise face as a south pole.
Like a bar magnet it has a magnetic moment m = NIA, aligns itself with an external field, and attracts or repels other magnets.
longQuestions: Consider a straight conductor of length L and cross-section A placed in a uniform field B at angle θ to the current. It contains n free charge carriers per unit volume, each of charge q moving with drift velocity v_d.
Force on one carrier: F₁ = qv_dB sin θ. Number of carriers in the conductor: N = nAL.
Total force: F = nAL q v_d B sin θ. Since the current is I = nAqv_d, F = ILB sin θ.
In vector form F = I L × B, where L points along the current. The force is perpendicular to both L and B (right-hand rule / Fleming's left-hand rule).
F is maximum (ILB) when the conductor is perpendicular to B and zero when it is parallel to B.
Take a rectangular coil of N turns, sides a (along the axis of rotation) and b, carrying current I in a uniform field B; let α be the angle between the plane of the coil and B.
The two sides of length b feel equal and opposite forces along the axis that cancel. The two sides of length a feel forces F = NIaB, equal, opposite and not in line — they form a couple.
Perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the couple: b cos α.
Torque: τ = F × b cos α = NIaB b cos α = NIAB cos α, where A = ab is the area.
If θ is the angle between the normal to the coil and B (θ = 90° − α), τ = NIAB sin θ, or τ = m × B with magnetic moment m = NIA. τ is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to B.
Yes. A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences the magnetic (Lorentz) force F = q v × B, of magnitude F = qvB sin θ.
The force is perpendicular to both v and B; its direction is given by the right-hand rule (reversed for a negative charge).
F = 0 if the charge is at rest or moves parallel to B; F is maximum (qvB) when v ⊥ B.
Because F ⊥ v, the force does no work: it changes the direction but not the speed. A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B moves in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB).
With an electric field also present, the total Lorentz force is F = qE + q v × B.
Electrons from a heated filament are accelerated through a potential difference V: ½mv² = eV, so v = √(2eV/m).
The beam enters a uniform magnetic field B (produced by Helmholtz coils) at right angles, so the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: evB = mv²/r, giving v = eBr/m.
Equating the two expressions for v: e²B²r²/m² = 2eV/m, so e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
The beam moves in a circle made visible by the gas in a fine-beam tube; V, B and the radius r are measured.
The accepted value is e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.
Magnetic flux Φ through a surface is the number of magnetic field lines passing through it; it is the scalar product of B and the vector area A: Φ = B · A = BA cos θ.
θ is the angle between B and the normal (vector area) of the surface.
Φ is maximum (BA) when the field is perpendicular to the surface (θ = 0°) and zero when it is parallel to the surface (θ = 90°).
SI unit: weber (Wb), 1 Wb = 1 T m² = 1 N m A⁻¹. Magnetic flux density B = Φ/A⊥, measured in tesla (Wb m⁻²).
For a non-uniform field or curved surface, Φ = ∫ B · dA.
Ampere's law: the line integral of B round any closed path equals μ₀ times the total current enclosed by the path: ∮ B · dl = μ₀I.
Solenoid: a long coil with n turns per unit length carrying current I. The field inside is uniform and parallel to the axis; outside it is nearly zero.
Choose a rectangular Amperian loop abcd: side ab of length l inside along the axis, cd outside, bc and da perpendicular to the axis.
Contributions: along ab, B l; along cd, 0 (B ≈ 0 outside); along bc and da, 0 (B ⊥ dl inside, B = 0 outside). So ∮ B · dl = Bl.
Current enclosed = (number of turns nl) × I. Hence Bl = μ₀nlI, so B = μ₀nI (or B = μ₀NI/L).

A galvanometer is a sensitive instrument for detecting and measuring small currents. A coil pivoted in a radial magnetic field turns until the deflecting torque NIAB balances the restoring torque cθ of the spring, so θ = (NAB/c) I ∝ I.

Ammeter: connect a small resistance (shunt) R_s in parallel. If the galvanometer (resistance R_g) gives full-scale deflection at I_g and the ammeter range is I, then I_gR_g = (I − I_g)R_s, so R_s = I_gR_g/(I − I_g). The ammeter has very low resistance and is joined in series in a circuit.
Voltmeter: connect a high resistance R_h in series. For range V: V = I_g(R_g + R_h), so R_h = V/I_g − R_g. The voltmeter has very high resistance and is joined in parallel across the component.
